claim: HUES8 primed hESCs were grown on Matrigel and dedifferentiated to naïve pluripotency using mTeSR-based medium supplemented with MEK (PD0325901) and GSK3 (CHIR99021) inhibitors, the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin, human leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), and ascorbic acid.
source: HUES8 primed hESCs were grown on Matrigel and dedifferentiated to naïve pluripotency using previously reported conditions in an mTeSR-based medium supplemented with MEK (PD0325901) and GSK3 (CHIR99021) inhibitors, the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin, human leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), and ascorbic acid (Duggal et al., 2015; Qin et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental protocol used for dedifferentiation, which is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Treatment with dedifferentiation medium induced colonies to develop a prominent dome-shape by day 6 of dedifferentiation.
source: We found that this treatment induced colonies to develop a prominent dome-shape by day 6 of dedifferentiation and increase expression of naïve pluripotency markers DNMT3L, DPPA3, KLF2, and KLF4, as determined by rt-PCR (Figure 1A and B), which confirms the transition to a naïve state.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and referenced to Figure 1A and B showing morphological changes.

claim: Treatment with dedifferentiation medium increased expression of naïve pluripotency markers DNMT3L, DPPA3, KLF2, and KLF4, as determined by rt-PCR.
source: We found that this treatment induced colonies to develop a prominent dome-shape by day 6 of dedifferentiation and increase expression of naïve pluripotency markers DNMT3L, DPPA3, KLF2, and KLF4, as determined by rt-PCR (Figure 1A and B), which confirms the transition to a naïve state.
evidence: The claim is supported by rt-PCR data showing increased expression of specific markers, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Naïve but not primed colonies had a ring of bundled actin filaments at the colony periphery.
source: Staining fixed cells for actin filaments with phalloidin revealed that naïve but not primed colonies had a ring of bundled actin filaments at the colony periphery (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A similar actin ring formed around colonies of naïve H9 cells and naïve WTC11 induced PSCs (iPSCs).
source: A similar actin ring also formed around colonies of naïve H9 cells and naïve WTC11 induced PSCs (iPSCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) as well as HUES8 cells dedifferentiated by alternative medium supplements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from multiple cell lines shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The actin ring assembled independently of naïve colony size.
source: Moreover, the actin ring assembled independently of naïve colony size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing actin rings in colonies of different sizes, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The actin filament ring around naïve hESC colonies was tethered to adherens junctions, as indicated by co-labeling for β-catenin.
source: The actin filament ring we observed around naïve hESC colonies was instead tethered to adherens junctions, as indicated by co-labeling for β-catenin, with separated interdigitated adherens junctions suggesting a contractile force (Figure 1D, crosshairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data showing co-localization of actin and β-catenin, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Separated interdigitated adherens junctions suggest a contractile force in naïve hESC colonies.
source: The actin filament ring we observed around naïve hESC colonies was instead tethered to adherens junctions, as indicated by co-labeling for β-catenin, with separated interdigitated adherens junctions suggesting a contractile force (Figure 1D, crosshairs).
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations from imaging data in Figure 1D.

claim: The actin ring around naïve hESC colonies was decorated with phosphorylated myosin light chain (pMLC).
source: The contractile property of the ring was also suggested by the actin ring around naïve hESC colonies being decorated with pMLC as determined by immunolabeling (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data showing pMLC localization, as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Primed hESC colonies had irregular aggregates of pMLC with limited co-localization with actin filaments.
source: In contrast, primed hESC colonies had irregular aggregates of pMLC with limited co-localization with actin filaments.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data comparing primed and naïve cells.

claim: Immunolabeling for cortactin partly overlapped with the actin ring in naïve hESC colonies.
source: Additionally, immunolabeling for cortactin, a regulator of cortical branched actin filaments, partly overlapped with the actin ring (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data showing cortactin localization, as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The actin ring is likely composed of unbranched actin filaments, which bind pMLC, and branched filaments, which bind cortactin.
source: Together, these data indicate a contractile actin ring surrounding naïve but not primed hESC colonies, with the ring likely composed of unbranched actin filaments, which bind pMLC, and branched filaments, which bind cortactin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-localization data of pMLC and cortactin with actin filaments, drawing on established knowledge about actin-binding proteins.

claim: Primed colonies exhibited elevated cell-substrate tractions that were distributed throughout the colony.
source: Consistent with pMLC localization, primed colonies exhibited elevated cell-substrate tractions that were distributed throughout the colony (Figure 1G, left; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Naïve colonies exhibited overall low magnitude cell-substrate tractions that were localized to the colony periphery and largely absent from the colony interior.
source: In contrast, naïve colonies exhibited overall low magnitude cell-substrate tractions that were localized to the colony periphery and largely absent from the colony interior (Figure 1G, right; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting decreased cell-substrate tensional force and a likely shift to more stabilized cell-cell forces.
evidence: The claim is supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Low traction forces in naïve colonies suggest decreased cell-substrate tensional force and a likely shift to more stabilized cell-cell forces.
source: In contrast, naïve colonies exhibited overall low magnitude cell-substrate tractions that were localized to the colony periphery and largely absent from the colony interior (Figure 1G, right; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting decreased cell-substrate tensional force and a likely shift to more stabilized cell-cell forces.
evidence: The claim is inferred from traction force microscopy data and pMLC localization patterns.

claim: The actin ring assembled when naïve cells are generated in the presence of SMIFH2, a broad-spectrum inhibitor of formin activity.
source: We found that the actin ring assembled when naïve cells are generated in the presence of SMIFH2, a broad-spectrum inhibitor of formin activity (Rizvi et al., 2009; Ganguly et al., 2015) but not CK666, a selective pharmacological inhibitor of Arp2/3 complex activity (Nolen et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2012 ; Figure 2A), despite the ring likely being composed of both unbranched and branched actin filaments as indicated by pMLC and cortactin immunolabeling.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing actin ring formation in the presence of SMIFH2, as shown in Figure 2A, and is supported by citations.

claim: The actin ring did not assemble when naïve cells are generated in the presence of CK666, a selective pharmacological inhibitor of Arp2/3 complex activity.
source: We found that the actin ring assembled when naïve cells are generated in the presence of SMIFH2, a broad-spectrum inhibitor of formin activity (Rizvi et al., 2009; Ganguly et al., 2015) but not CK666, a selective pharmacological inhibitor of Arp2/3 complex activity (Nolen et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2012 ; Figure 2A), despite the ring likely being composed of both unbranched and branched actin filaments as indicated by pMLC and cortactin immunolabeling.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing lack of actin ring formation in the presence of CK666, as shown in Figure 2A, and is supported by citations.

claim: CK666 blocked increased expression of markers of naïve pluripotency PECAM1, ESRRB, KLF4, and DNMT3L.
source: Additionally, CK666 blocked increased expression of markers of naïve pluripotency seen in controls, determined by quantitative PCR (qPCR) of PECAM1, ESRRB, KLF4, and DNMT3L (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CK666-treated cells remained broadly pluripotent as indicated by immunolabeling for OCT4 and SOX2.
source: To eliminate the possibility that CK666 treatment led cells to exit pluripotency and differentiate, we immunolabeled for the general pluripotency markers OCT4 and SOX2 and found that CK666-treated cells remained broadly pluripotent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: CK869, another inhibitor of Arp2/3 complex activity, blocked the formation of the actin ring without impairing pluripotency.
source: To further confirm that Arp2/3 complex activity is necessary for the actin filament ring, we also treated cells with CK869, another inhibitor of Arp2/3 complex activity (Hetrick et al., 2013) . Consistent with our finding using CK666, CK869 blocked the formation of the actin ring without impairing pluripotency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, and is supported by a citation.

claim: SSEA3 expression significantly decreased with dedifferentiation in control conditions.
source: SSEA3 expression significantly decreased with dedifferentiation in control conditions, as previously reported (Liu et al., 2017) but remained at levels similar to primed cells in the presence of CK666 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2C and D, and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SSEA3 expression remained at levels similar to primed cells in the presence of CK666.
source: SSEA3 expression significantly decreased with dedifferentiation in control conditions, as previously reported (Liu et al., 2017) but remained at levels similar to primed cells in the presence of CK666 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The naïve pluripotency marker KLF4 translocated from the cytoplasm to the nucleus with control dedifferentiation but not in the presence of CK666.
source: Additionally, the naïve pluripotency marker KLF4 (Takashima et al., 2014) translocated from the cytoplasm to the nucleus with control dedifferentiation but not in the presence of CK666 (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2C and E, and is supported by a citation.

claim: There was no difference in EdU incorporation in the absence or presence of CK666 or CK869.
source: Although branched actin filaments generated by Arp2/3 complex promote cell cycle progression and proliferation (Molinie et al., 2019), we used an EdU pulse (1 hour) to show no difference in EdU incorporation in the absence or presence of CK666 or CK869 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the inhibitors did not change cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, and is supported by a citation.

claim: CK666 disrupted localization of cortactin around naïve colonies.
source: Consistent with CK666 disrupting the actin filament ring, it also disrupted localization of cortactin around naïve colonies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Colony formation was greater in naïve compared with primed hESC in controls.
source: In controls, colony formation was greater in naïve compared with primed hESC, as previously reported (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: With CK666 but not CK689, an inactive analog of CK666, there was no increase in colony formation in naïve compared with primed cells.
source: However, with CK666 but not CK689, an inactive analog of CK666, there was no increase in colony formation in naïve compared with primed cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Elevated cell-substrate tractions throughout colonies of primed but not naïve cells were retained when hESCs were dedifferentiated in the presence of CK666.
source: Additionally, traction force microscopy revealed that elevated cell-substrate tractions throughout colonies of primed but not naïve cells (Figure 1G) were retained when hESCs were dedifferentiated in the presence of CK666 (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Arp2/3 complex activity is essential for promoting an actin filament ring and uniform naïve colony mechanics.
source: These data identify an essential role for the Arp2/3 complex in promoting an actin filament ring and uniform naïve colony mechanics as well as acquiring a naïve pluripotent state in hESCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing effects of Arp2/3 inhibition on actin ring formation and colony mechanics.

claim: Arp2/3 complex activity is essential for acquiring a naïve pluripotent state in hESCs.
source: These data identify an essential role for the Arp2/3 complex in promoting an actin filament ring and uniform naïve colony mechanics as well as acquiring a naïve pluripotent state in hESCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing effects of Arp2/3 inhibition on naïve pluripotency markers and colony formation.

claim: Primed, naïve, and CK666-treated cells had a total of 12,817 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with an adjusted pval<0.05.
source: We found that primed, naïve, and CK666-treated cells had a total of 12,817 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with an adjusted pval<0.05 (false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected by Benjamini-Hochberg procedure).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis data.

claim: 182 DEGs were unique to control primed cells compared with control naïve cells and were not differentially expressed in CK666-treated cells.
source: Of these DEGs, 182 were unique to control primed cells compared with control naïve cells and were not differentially expressed in CK666-treated cells; CK666-treated cells compared with control primed or control naïve cells had 102 and 502 DEGs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis data.

claim: CK666-treated cells compared with control primed or control naïve cells had 102 and 502 DEGs, respectively.
source: Of these DEGs, 182 were unique to control primed cells compared with control naïve cells and were not differentially expressed in CK666-treated cells; CK666-treated cells compared with control primed or control naïve cells had 102 and 502 DEGs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis data.

claim: Hippo signaling was the top candidate pathway in control naïve dedifferentiation identified by KEGG pathway analysis.
source: To determine the transcriptional networks involved in the dedifferentiation from primed to naïve pluripotency, we identified KEGG pathways in control naïve dedifferentiation which revealed Hippo signaling as the top candidate (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TEAD2 was one of the top candidates in transcription factor binding motif analysis.
source: Additionally, transcription factor binding motif analysis revealed that one of the top candidates was TEAD2 (Figure 3C), which is a downstream effector of Hippo signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcription factor enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TEAD2 is a downstream effector of Hippo signaling.
source: Additionally, transcription factor binding motif analysis revealed that one of the top candidates was TEAD2 (Figure 3C), which is a downstream effector of Hippo signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the Hippo signaling pathway.

claim: Of the 3744 YAP target genes identified in the RNAseq dataset, 3156 (84%) were not differentially expressed in any condition and 588 (16%) were enriched in one or multiple conditions.
source: For an unbiased global analysis of known YAP target genes, we used two publicly available datasets (Estarás et al., 2017; Pagliari et al., 2021) and found that of the 3744 YAP target genes identified in our RNAseq dataset, 3156 (84%) were not differentially expressed in any condition and 588 (16%) were enriched in one or multiple conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis using publicly available YAP target gene datasets.

claim: Of the 588 enriched YAP target genes, 174 (30%) were significantly enriched in the control naïve dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition.
source: Of those 588 enriched YAP target genes, 174 (30%) were significantly enriched in the control naïve dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition; 407 (69%) were significantly enriched among CK666-treated dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition; and 7 (1%) were significantly enriched in both conditions versus the control primed condition (Figure 3D, adjusted pval>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 407 (69%) of enriched YAP target genes were significantly enriched among CK666-treated dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition.
source: Of those 588 enriched YAP target genes, 174 (30%) were significantly enriched in the control naïve dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition; 407 (69%) were significantly enriched among CK666-treated dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition; and 7 (1%) were significantly enriched in both conditions versus the control primed condition (Figure 3D, adjusted pval>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 7 (1%) of enriched YAP target genes were significantly enriched in both control naïve and CK666-treated conditions versus the control primed condition.
source: Of those 588 enriched YAP target genes, 174 (30%) were significantly enriched in the control naïve dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition; 407 (69%) were significantly enriched among CK666-treated dedifferentiation condition versus the control primed condition; and 7 (1%) were significantly enriched in both conditions versus the control primed condition (Figure 3D, adjusted pval>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Known naïve pluripotency markers such as OTX2, DLG2, and CRY1 were significantly upregulated in control naïve condition compared with control primed condition.
source: Of the genes significantly enriched in the control naïve condition compared with the control primed condition, known naïve pluripotency markers such as OTX2, DLG2, and CRY1 were significantly upregulated, and these naïve markers were not significantly increased in CK666-treated cells (Figure 3E, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Naïve markers OTX2, DLG2, and CRY1 were not significantly increased in CK666-treated cells.
source: Of the genes significantly enriched in the control naïve condition compared with the control primed condition, known naïve pluripotency markers such as OTX2, DLG2, and CRY1 were significantly upregulated, and these naïve markers were not significantly increased in CK666-treated cells (Figure 3E, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Genes significantly enriched among both control naïve and CK666-treated conditions included known YAP and Hippo targets such as ANKRD1, SLIT2, and CHD10.
source: As expected, genes significantly enriched among both DEG lists included known YAP and Hippo targets such as ANKRD1, SLIT2, and CHD10 (Figure 3E, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Genes significantly enriched among the CK666-treated condition include the negative Hippo regulator AMOT.
source: Genes significantly enriched among the CK666-treated condition include the negative Hippo regulator AMOT (Zhao et al., 2011), and lineage-commitment genes such as SOX6 and SPEF2 (Figure 3E, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 3E and is supported by a citation.

claim: Genes significantly enriched among the CK666-treated condition include lineage-commitment genes such as SOX6 and SPEF2.
source: Genes significantly enriched among the CK666-treated condition include the negative Hippo regulator AMOT (Zhao et al., 2011), and lineage-commitment genes such as SOX6 and SPEF2 (Figure 3E, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios of YAP with control dedifferentiation was blocked by CK666.
source: To verify this prediction, we immunolabeled cells to determine YAP localization and found increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios of YAP (Figure 3F and G) and TAZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) with control dedifferentiation that was blocked by CK666.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios of TAZ with control dedifferentiation was blocked by CK666.
source: To verify this prediction, we immunolabeled cells to determine YAP localization and found increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios of YAP (Figure 3F and G) and TAZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) with control dedifferentiation that was blocked by CK666.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Immunoblotting total cell lysates for total YAP abundance indicated no difference between primed and naïve hESCs.
source: Immunoblotting total cell lysates for total YAP abundance indicated no difference between primed and naïve hESCs and a small but significant increase in hESCs treated with CK666 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Immunoblotting total cell lysates for total YAP abundance indicated a small but significant increase in hESCs treated with CK666.
source: Immunoblotting total cell lysates for total YAP abundance indicated no difference between primed and naïve hESCs and a small but significant increase in hESCs treated with CK666 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Actin filaments and associated proteins generate mechanical forces during preimplantation development that contribute to differentiation throughout the blastocyst stage by modulating mechanosensitive pathways such as Hippo.
source: Consistent with our findings, actin filaments and associated proteins generate mechanical forces during preimplantation development that contribute to differentiation throughout the blastocyst stage by modulating mechanosensitive pathways such as Hippo (Hirate et al., 2015; Zenker et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Actin structures allow cells within the developing blastocyst to organize based on contractility, coupling mechanosensing, and fate specification.
source: These actin structures allow cells within the developing blastocyst to organize based on contractility, coupling mechanosensing, and fate specification (Maître et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of YAP-S127A in the presence of CK666 restored increased nuclear localization of KLF4.
source: Accordingly, we found that that expression of YAP-S127A in the presence of CK666 restored two markers of the naïve state, increased nuclear localization of KLF4 (Figure 4A and B) and decreased SSEA3 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Expression of YAP-S127A in the presence of CK666 restored decreased SSEA3.
source: Accordingly, we found that that expression of YAP-S127A in the presence of CK666 restored two markers of the naïve state, increased nuclear localization of KLF4 (Figure 4A and B) and decreased SSEA3 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Acquisition of a naïve pluripotency state remained blocked with CK666 treatment in cells overexpressing wildtype YAP (YAP-WT).
source: In contrast, acquisition of a naïve pluripotency state remained blocked with CK666 treatment in cells overexpressing wildtype YAP (YAP-WT) (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Colony formation was restored by heterologous expression of YAP-S127A but not YAP-WT in the presence of CK666.
source: Colony formation, a functional form of naïve pluripotency, was also restored by heterologous expression of YAP-S127A but not YAP-WT in the presence of CK666 (Figure 4E), indicating that Arp2/3 complex activity is necessary for active nuclear-localized YAP to induce a naïve pluripotency state.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Arp2/3 complex activity is necessary for active nuclear-localized YAP to induce a naïve pluripotency state.
source: Colony formation, a functional form of naïve pluripotency, was also restored by heterologous expression of YAP-S127A but not YAP-WT in the presence of CK666 (Figure 4E), indicating that Arp2/3 complex activity is necessary for active nuclear-localized YAP to induce a naïve pluripotency state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiment showing that constitutively active YAP restores naïve pluripotency when Arp2/3 is inhibited.

claim: Expressing YAP-S127A but not YAP-WT in the presence of CK666 partially restored a contractile actin ring enclosing naïve cell colonies.
source: In addition, we found that expressing YAP-S127A but not YAP-WT in the presence of CK666 partially restored a contractile actin ring enclosing naïve cell colonies (Figure 4F), indicating bidirectional signaling between actin filament remodeling and active nuclear-localized YAP for assembly of the actin filament ring around naïve hESC colonies.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There is bidirectional signaling between actin filament remodeling and active nuclear-localized YAP for assembly of the actin filament ring around naïve hESC colonies.
source: In addition, we found that expressing YAP-S127A but not YAP-WT in the presence of CK666 partially restored a contractile actin ring enclosing naïve cell colonies (Figure 4F), indicating bidirectional signaling between actin filament remodeling and active nuclear-localized YAP for assembly of the actin filament ring around naïve hESC colonies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that YAP-S127A can partially restore the actin ring when Arp2/3 is inhibited, suggesting YAP acts downstream of actin remodeling but also feeds back to regulate it.

claim: The transition from primed to naïve hESC pluripotency includes an Arp2/3 complex-dependent actin filament remodeling that enables active nuclear-localized YAP.
source: Thus, we conclude that both the transition from primed to naïve hESC pluripotency includes an Arp2/3 complex-dependent actin filament remodeling that enables active nuclear-localized YAP, and that nuclear-localized YAP enables actin filament remodeling for naïve pluripotency.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data showing the relationship between Arp2/3 activity, actin remodeling, and YAP localization.

claim: Nuclear-localized YAP enables actin filament remodeling for naïve pluripotency.
source: Thus, we conclude that both the transition from primed to naïve hESC pluripotency includes an Arp2/3 complex-dependent actin filament remodeling that enables active nuclear-localized YAP, and that nuclear-localized YAP enables actin filament remodeling for naïve pluripotency.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data showing that YAP-S127A can partially restore actin ring formation.

claim: Naïve pluripotency is characterized by an Arp2/3 complex-dependent remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton that includes formation of a contractile actin ring enclosing naïve colonies.
source: Our new findings support a model in which naïve pluripotency is characterized by an Arp2/3 complex-dependent remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton that includes formation of a contractile actin ring enclosing naïve colonies and establishment of uniform tensional forces in colonies likely enabled by the actin ring being physically associated with β-catenin and pMLC, which are known to play roles in pluripotency (Xu et al., 2016; De Belly et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings supported by the experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Naïve pluripotency is characterized by establishment of uniform tensional forces in colonies likely enabled by the actin ring being physically associated with β-catenin and pMLC.
source: Our new findings support a model in which naïve pluripotency is characterized by an Arp2/3 complex-dependent remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton that includes formation of a contractile actin ring enclosing naïve colonies and establishment of uniform tensional forces in colonies likely enabled by the actin ring being physically associated with β-catenin and pMLC, which are known to play roles in pluripotency (Xu et al., 2016; De Belly et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the traction force microscopy data and immunolabeling showing co-localization of actin with β-catenin and pMLC, supported by citations.

claim: β-catenin and pMLC are known to play roles in pluripotency.
source: Our new findings support a model in which naïve pluripotency is characterized by an Arp2/3 complex-dependent remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton that includes formation of a contractile actin ring enclosing naïve colonies and establishment of uniform tensional forces in colonies likely enabled by the actin ring being physically associated with β-catenin and pMLC, which are known to play roles in pluripotency (Xu et al., 2016; De Belly et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Arp2/3 activity facilitates dedifferentiation to a naïve state of pluripotency through promoting nuclear translocation of YAP and regulating Hippo target gene expression.
source: Moreover, Arp2/3 activity facilitates dedifferentiation to a naïve state of pluripotency through promoting nuclear translocation of YAP and regulating Hippo target gene expression.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings supported by the experimental data on YAP localization and RNA-sequencing analysis.

claim: The transition to naïve pluripotency is blocked with inhibiting Arp2/3 complex activity.
source: Consistent with these findings, whereas the transition to naïve pluripotency is blocked with inhibiting Arp2/3 complex activity, this transition is restored by expression of a constitutively active, nuclear-localized YAP-S127A.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing effects of CK666 on naïve pluripotency markers.

claim: The transition to naïve pluripotency is restored by expression of a constitutively active, nuclear-localized YAP-S127A when Arp2/3 complex activity is inhibited.
source: Consistent with these findings, whereas the transition to naïve pluripotency is blocked with inhibiting Arp2/3 complex activity, this transition is restored by expression of a constitutively active, nuclear-localized YAP-S127A.
evidence: The claim is supported by the rescue experiment data showing YAP-S127A restores naïve markers and colony formation.

claim: The contractile rings described are distinct from those that assemble around Xenopus neural crest cells, which function to enhance migratory capacity.
source: The contractile rings we describe are distinct from those that assemble around Xenopus neural crest cells (Shellard et al., 2018), which function to enhance migratory capacity, and around colonies of iPSCs (Närvä et al., 2017), which function to enhance cell-substrate adhesion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work describing different types of contractile rings.

claim: The contractile rings described are distinct from those that assemble around colonies of iPSCs, which function to enhance cell-substrate adhesion.
source: The contractile rings we describe are distinct from those that assemble around Xenopus neural crest cells (Shellard et al., 2018), which function to enhance migratory capacity, and around colonies of iPSCs (Närvä et al., 2017), which function to enhance cell-substrate adhesion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work describing different types of contractile rings.

claim: Induced pluripotency has long been proposed to be closer to naïve pluripotency than primed stem cells as conventionally isolated and maintained.
source: Induced pluripotency has long been proposed to be closer to naïve pluripotency than primed stem cells as conventionally isolated and maintained (Nichols and Smith, 2009; Theunissen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cells within the ICM of mouse blastocysts exclude YAP from the nucleus.
source: Cells within the ICM of mouse blastocysts exclude YAP from the nucleus whereas cells within the ICM of human blastocysts maintain nuclear YAP (Qin et al., 2016; Nishioka et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cells within the ICM of human blastocysts maintain nuclear YAP.
source: Cells within the ICM of mouse blastocysts exclude YAP from the nucleus whereas cells within the ICM of human blastocysts maintain nuclear YAP (Qin et al., 2016; Nishioka et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Murine naïve PSCs have predominantly cytosolic YAP.
